sec.title: Background
sec.p: Savolitinib, a potent MET inhibitor, showed promising efficacy and tolerable safety in a Phase 3b confirmatory trial for the treatment of Chinese patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harbouring MET exon 14 (METex14)-skipping mutations. Herein, we report the final trial results.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This multicentre, open-label, non-randomised, confirmatory Phase 3b study at 48 Chinese hospitals used a single-arm design. Eligible patients received savolitinib 400 mg (body weight <50 kg) or 600 mg (body weight ≥50 kg). Previously treated and treatment-naïve cohorts had a once-daily dosing frequency. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) assessed by an Independent Review Committee (IRC) per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours v1·1 criteria. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04923945, and has been completed.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: From Aug 31, 2021, to Nov 30, 2024, 166 patients were enrolled. In previously treated patients (N = 79), median follow-up was 25·1 months; IRC-assessed ORR, 42% (95% confidence interval [CI] 31%–53%); IRC-assessed median PFS, 13·7 months (95% CI 8·3–17·9), and median OS, 25·3 months (95% CI 20·5–30·5). Among treatment-naïve patients (N = 87), with a median follow-up of 34·5 months, ORR was 62% (95% CI 51%–72%); PFS, 13·7 months (95% CI 8·5–16·6); and OS, 28·3 months (95% CI 17·5–not estimated). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 62% of patients and were manageable.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: Savolitinib demonstrated robust and durable efficacy in patients with METex14-mutated, locally advanced NSCLC with manageable safety, supporting savolitinib as a treatment option in this disease setting.

sec.title: Evidence before this study
sec.p: The MET exon 14 mutation occurs in approximately 3%–4% of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is associated with aggressive disease and poor prognosis. Two selective MET inhibitors, capmatinib and tepotinib, have established efficacy in this setting, with pivotal studies reporting objective response rates of 68% and 44% for capmatinib and 57% and 45% for tepotinib in treatment-naïve and previously treated patients, respectively. In a Phase 2 pivotal study conducted in Chinese patients, savolitinib, a potent and highly selective MET inhibitor, demonstrated an Independent Review Committee-assessed objective response rate of 49% and median progression-free survival of 6·8 months, supporting conditional regulatory approval.

sec.title: Added value of this study
sec.p: This confirmatory Phase 3b trial is the first in China to comprehensively evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of savolitinib across two distinct cohorts: previously treated and treatment-naïve patients with MET exon 14-mutated NSCLC. The final analysis confirms clinically meaningful and durable responses in both groups. The median overall survival was 25·3 months and 28·3 months in previously treated and treatment-naïve populations, respectively, demonstrating long-term survival benefit.

sec.title: Implications of all the available evidence
sec.p: Savolitinib is a promising treatment option for patients with MET exon 14-mutated NSCLC, a population with limited treatment options. These confirmatory findings supported its full approval in China in January 2025 and validate the clinical relevance of routine genomic profiling and targeted MET inhibition in NSCLC. Savolitinib showed encouraging activity in patients with brain metastases, a subgroup with poor outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with mesenchymal epithelial transition factor (MET) exon mutations face unmet treatment needs. The MET exon 14 (METex14) mutation is a distinct oncogenic driver in NSCLC, albeit with a relatively low incidence of only 3%–4%.1 Patients with this specific mutation present with characteristic clinical features, often being elderly (median age approximately 70 years) and typically diagnosed with advanced (Stage IV) disease.2 Although conventional chemotherapy is the historical standard of care, NSCLC with METex14 mutations exhibits notable insensitivity to traditional chemotherapy, demonstrates poor responses to immunotherapy, and is associated with rapid tumour progression and a generally poor prognosis.3 Owing to the low co-occurrence with other common driver mutations, alternative targeted therapies are often not applicable to this distinct patient population, underscoring an urgent clinical need for novel, effective therapeutic agents.4

Ethnic and regional differences in the prevalence of driver mutations characterise the molecular epidemiology of NSCLC. Specifically, the prevalence of MET alterations, including METex14 skipping mutation, has been reported to have a distinct frequency in Chinese patients with NSCLC, differing from Western populations.5,6 Beyond genetic mutations, variations in drug metabolism due to polymorphic genes encoding enzymes like those in the cytochrome P450 (CYP) superfamily can influence drug pharmacokinetics, efficacy, and toxicity profiles.7 The frequency of these CYP enzyme polymorphisms can vary significantly between populations, such as those of Asian, African, and European descent.8

In recent years, the landscape of METex14-mutated NSCLC treatment has evolved with the availability of MET inhibitors. Tepotinib and capmatinib are well-established MET inhibitors for NSCLC. The results of pivotal studies for capmatinib9 and tepotinib10 have demonstrated robust efficacy, with objective response rates (ORRs) of 44% and 68% for capmatinib and 45% and 57% for tepotinib10 in previously treated and treatment-naïve patients, respectively. Consistent with these findings, pooled results across studies show ORRs of 41%–50% in previously treated patients, with median progression-free survival (PFS) of 5·4–11·5 months and overall survival (OS) of 13·6–26·0 months; in treatment-naïve patients, these results were 57%–69%, 10·3–15·9 months, and 17·6–29·7 months, respectively.9, 10, 11, 12 Other investigational MET inhibitors, such as glumetinib and vebreltinib, have shown encouraging activity in single-arm studies conducted in China.13,14

Within a similar context, savolitinib, a highly selective small molecule MET inhibitor, showed promising preliminary efficacy in its Phase 2 pivotal study,15 with an Independent Review Committee (IRC)-assessed ORR of 49%, and a median PFS of 6·8 months. These preliminary Phase 2 results15 led to conditional approval in China in 2021 for adults with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with METex14-skipping mutations who progressed on or were intolerant to platinum-based chemotherapy.

The present confirmatory study aimed to verify the efficacy and safety of savolitinib in patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with METex14-skipping mutations. The positive results from the primary analysis data (20 October 2023, data cutoff)16,17 led to the full approval of savolitinib in January 2025 for this disease setting. As of 30 November 2024, with the last patient followed up for over 12 months, the present manuscript summarises the final analysis of this confirmatory study.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This was a single-arm, multi-cohort, multicentre, open-label Phase 3b study. The detailed methodology has been published.16 The screening and enrolment of patients were performed at 48 study sites across China. The study comprised a screening period, a treatment period, and a follow-up period. The data cutoff for the present analysis was 30 November 2024.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: The eligible population consisted of adults (≥18 years) with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC; with METex14 mutations (detected by local or central laboratory testing); without epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), and c-Ros proto-oncogene 1 (ROS1) sensitive mutations; who had not received previous treatment targeting cellular-mesenchymal epithelial transition factor (c-MET); who had adequate organ function; who had Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1; and who had measurable tumours per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1·1. In the central laboratory, METex14-skipping mutations were analysed in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded samples using a next-generation sequencing panel (Tetradecan 14-gene panel, Geneseeq Technology, Nanjing, China). Sex was recorded as a biological variable based on medical records at enrolment; gender identity/gender-related variables were not collected.

Patients were excluded if they had previously received anti-MET therapy; had gene mutations sensitive to targeted drugs for EGFR, ALK, or ROS1; had unstable brain metastasis requiring glucocorticoid or antiepileptic treatment; or had presence of active cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, liver, or any other disease or condition that was not suitable for the study drug that would affect the interpretation of the study results or put the patient at high risk.

Patients meeting the eligibility criteria were included in one of three cohorts based on their prior antitumour therapy for advanced disease. The previously treated cohort consisted of patients who experienced progressive disease (PD) or intolerable toxicity following prior platinum-based chemotherapy. The treatment-naïve cohort included patients who had not previously received any drug therapy for advanced tumours. Additionally, the dosage exploration cohort included treatment-naïve patients receiving different dosing frequencies.
This report focuses on the data analysis corresponding to the previously treated and treatment-naïve cohorts. The dosage exploration cohort data were exploratory and will be reported separately.

sec.title: Treatment and follow-up
sec.p: Treatment consisted of the approved dosing regimen of savolitinib15 for the previously treated and treatment-naïve cohorts. Patients with baseline weight ≥50 kg received savolitinib 600 mg orally once daily (QD) and continuously. For patients with baseline weight <50 kg, savolitinib was administered at a dose of 400 mg orally QD until disease progression, death, intolerable toxicity, or other termination criteria as specified in the protocol, whichever occurred first.

Tumour assessments using computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging were performed at baseline, once every 6 weeks (±7 days) from the first dose of savolitinib until week 48, and every 12 weeks (±7 days) thereafter. An IRC and investigators separately evaluated the tumour responses via RECIST 1·1.18 Survival follow-up was performed once every 12 weeks (±7 days) after the end of treatment, during which patients were followed up via phone to assess their survival status and subsequent antitumour therapies.

sec.title: Study endpoints
sec.p: The efficacy endpoints were ORR assessed by IRC (RECIST 1·1 criteria),18 ORR evaluated by the investigator, PFS (RECIST 1·1 criteria), PFS rate at 6 months, disease control rate (DCR), time to response (TTR), duration of response (DoR), and OS. The safety endpoints were the severity and incidence of various adverse events (AEs), and changes in results of laboratory examinations, vital signs, and 12-lead electrocardiography from baseline by visit throughout the treatment.

sec.title: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) exploratory biomarker analysis
sec.p: Plasma samples were prospectively collected at baseline, and ctDNA was extracted from plasma using the QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany). Gene alterations were detected by next-generation sequencing (Pulmocan, 139-gene panel; Geneseeq Technology). Variant calling entailed the use of VarScan2 and ADTEx to detect somatic mutations, and coexisting gene alterations at baseline were identified.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Formal statistical hypothesis testing was performed based on a two-sided exact 95% confidence interval (CI) for the IRC-assessed ORR using a one-sided α level of 0·025 for both the previously treated cohort and treatment-naïve cohort. For the previously treated cohort, a 25% ORR was considered clinically meaningful. The null hypothesis (ORR ≤25%) was rejected if the lower bound of the two-sided exact 95% CI exceeded 25%, on which basis savolitinib was considered effective. Assuming a true ORR of 40% based on Phase 2 data,15 a sample size of 78 patients would yield 80% power to reject the null hypothesis.

For the treatment-naïve cohort, the sample size consideration has been published.16 In this cohort, a 35% ORR was considered clinically meaningful. The null hypothesis (ORR ≤35%) was rejected if the lower bound of the two-sided exact 95% CI exceeded 35%, on which basis savolitinib was considered effective.

As of 20 October 2023, the data cutoff for the primary analysis, efficacy was determined when the lower limit of the 95% CI for the IRC-assessed ORRs exceeded the null threshold for both the previously treated cohort (ORR of 39% [95% CI 28%, 51%]) and treatment-naïve cohort (ORR of 62% [95% CI 51%, 72%]).16,17

On 30 November 2024 (data cutoff for final analysis), the last enrolled patient was followed up for more than 12 months, meeting the criteria for end of study. Thus, this final analysis was performed.

The present analysis reports on data collected in the full analysis set (FAS), which included all patients who had received at least one dose of the study medication. Continuous variables were summarised by standard descriptive statistics (median, range). Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages. Kaplan–Meier analysis was used for time-to-event variables (PFS, TTR, DoR, OS) to calculate median, quartiles, and 95% CIs, with results displayed as curves. The Clopper–Pearson method was used to calculate the corresponding exact 95% CIs for ORR and DCR. All analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise® Software version 8·3 or higher (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).
A post hoc subgroup analysis focusing on efficacy endpoints was conducted for patients with stable brain metastases at baseline as well as those who developed brain metastases during the study.

An exploratory biomarker analysis was conducted to examine treatment efficacy based on concurrent gene alterations in baseline ctDNA samples. We conducted a concordance analysis to compare METex14 detection in ctDNA with original tissue biopsy results. Clinical outcomes were compared using the chi-square test and unstratified log-rank tests, separately for ORR and PFS/OS between groups with different METex14 alterations.

sec.title: Ethics approval
sec.p: The protocol was approved by the institutional review board at each study site, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and adhered to Good Clinical Practice guidelines. All patients provided informed consent before enrolment. The initial study protocol and all subsequent amendments were reviewed and approved by the independent ethics committee for each hospital (Supplementary Table S1). The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov under the identifier number NCT04923945 on May 30, 2021.

sec.title: Role of the funding source
sec.p: HUTCHMED had a role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, and writing of the report, and in the decision to submit the paper for publication. AstraZeneca had no role in the above-mentioned procedures but reviewed a draft of this manuscript.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p:
The patient disposition in the previously treated and treatment-naïve cohorts is shown in Fig. 1. In the previously treated cohort, 79 of 107 screened patients were enrolled and received savolitinib. At the data cutoff, with a median follow-up of 25·1 months (95% CI 22·3–28·6), all patients discontinued savolitinib, primarily because of PD (59%) and study completion as determined by the sponsor (19%). In the treatment-naïve cohort, 87 of the 125 patients screened were enrolled and received savolitinib. At data cutoff, with a median follow-up of 34·5 months (95% CI 33·1–35·2), all patients discontinued savolitinib, predominantly because of PD (56%) and study completion as determined by the sponsor (14%). All 79 patients in the previously treated cohort and 87 patients in the treatment-naïve cohort were included in the FAS.Fig. 1
Patient disposition.a Other reasons included refusal to undergo overall survival follow-up (1 patient), and inability to undergo examination at the study site within the screening window because of the COVID-19 epidemic (1 patient).

In the previously treated cohort, patients had a median (range) age of 68·8 (50·6–82·5) years, 57% were male, and 59% were non-smokers (Table 1). Most patients had advanced-stage NSCLC at screening (Stage IV, 91%). The most common histological subtype was adenocarcinoma (78%), and brain metastases were documented in 27% of patients. The characteristics of the treatment-naïve cohort have been published.16 Briefly, patients in this cohort had a median (range) age of 70·0 (51·2–87·8) years, most patients were male (59%), and 62% were non-smokers. Most patients (89%) were at Stage IV at screening. Adenocarcinoma was the most common histological subtype (80%), and brain metastases were seen in 11% of patients.Table 1

Other types included: adenocarcinoma mixed with pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma, possible squamous carcinoma (one patient each from the previously treated cohort); poorly differentiated non-small cell carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer (one patient each from the treatment-naïve cohort).

Subsequent antitumour therapies were administered to 42 (53%) patients in the previously treated cohort and 47 (54%) in the treatment-naïve cohort. In both cohorts, subsequent systemic therapies predominantly included targeted therapy (23% in previously treated patients; 23% in treatment-naïve patients), chemotherapy (9% in previously treated patients; 16% in treatment-naïve patients), and combinations (Supplementary Table S2). Notably, subsequent immunotherapy was less common (4% in previously treated patients; 3% in treatment-naïve patients) in this study.

sec.title: Study endpoints
sec.p:
As assessed by IRC, in the previously treated cohort (FAS), the confirmed ORR was 42% (95% CI 31%–53%) and the DCR was 92% (95% CI 84%–97%) (Table 2). The median DoR was 11·1 months (95% CI 7·6–20·7) and the median TTR was 1·6 months (95% CI 1·4–2·8). In total, 47 (59%) patients had PD or death without progression. In the treatment-naïve cohort (FAS), the efficacy results at this final analysis were generally consistent with those published in the primary analysis. In brief, based on the IRC assessment, ORR and DCR were 62% and 92%, respectively. The median DoR was 12·4 months (95% CI 8·3–18·0), and the median TTR was 1·4 months (95% CI 1·4–1·5). The median PFS was 13·7 months (95% CI 8·5–16·6; Fig. 2b), and the 6-month PFS rate was 72% (95% CI 61%–80%). The efficacy results based on investigator assessments were generally consistent with the assessments by the IRC. Tumour shrinkage in each cohort by IRC assessment after study treatment is shown in Supplementary Figure S1.

In the previously treated cohort, the median duration of follow-up for OS was 25·1 months (95% CI 22·3–28·6), and 41 (52%) patients died. The median OS was 25·3 months (95% CI 20·5–30·5). In the treatment-naïve cohort, the median duration of follow-up for OS was 34·5 months (95% CI 33·1–35·2), and 47 (54%) patients died. The median OS was 28·3 months (95% CI 17·5–not estimated [NE]) (Fig. 2c and d).

In the previously treated cohort, 21 patients had baseline brain metastases based on investigator assessment. The confirmed ORR in these 21 patients by IRC was 33% (95% CI 15%–57%; Supplementary Table S3). When evaluating the intracranial activity in the 21 patients with baseline brain metastases, three patients had measurable brain target lesions and two patients presented with lesion shrinkage to 5 mm before the cutoff date; 19 patients had non-target brain lesions and six of them achieved complete disappearance, although one of these six relapsed 12 weeks later (two tumour–assessment cycles). Of the 21 patients, one experienced intracranial progression and two developed new brain metastases. In the treatment-naïve cohort, 10 patients had baseline brain metastases. The confirmed ORR by IRC was 50% (95% CI 19%–81%). None of these patients appeared to present with intracranial disease progression.

Exploratory analysis by histological subtype (Supplementary Table S4) showed numerically lower efficacy in squamous cell carcinoma versus adenocarcinoma. However, small subgroup sizes (N = 7 previously treated; N = 5 treatment-naïve) preclude definitive conclusions.

Exploratory efficacy analyses examined METex14 alterations by region (splice donor versus splice acceptor versus other) and type (base substitution versus indels) in both previously treated and treatment-naive cohorts (Supplementary Tables S5 and S6). The distribution of alteration regions and types was similar between cohorts, with no significant differences observed in ORR, median PFS, or median OS across these molecular subgroups.

Among the enrolled patients, 77 (57 and 20 from the previously treated and treatment-naïve cohorts, respectively) with baseline ctDNA samples were analyzed for concurrent gene alterations (Fig. 3). METex14 was detected in 91% of patients, demonstrating high concordance between tissue and ctDNA for METex14 detection. Coexisting gene alterations were mainly found in the components of the RTK-MAPK-PI3K, cell cycle, DNA damage, and epigenetics regulation pathways. The most frequent genomic alteration coexisting with METex14-skipping mutation was TP53 (30%) in 23 of 77 patients, followed by DNMT3A (9%), BRIP1 (6%), AXL (6%), and GNAS (6%). TP53 remained the most common co-mutation in both previously treated (30%, 17/57) and treatment-naïve patients with NSCLC (30%, 6/20). ORR, PFS, and OS were comparable between patients with and without TP53 mutations (Supplementary Table S7). In the pooled population, the ORR was 48% (11 of 23 patients) versus 46% (25 of 54 patients), median PFS was 13·8 months versus 13·8 months, and median OS was 25·9 months versus 29·1 months, in patients with and without TP53 mutations, respectively.Fig. 3

The proportion of patients who experienced at least one treatment-related AE (TRAE) was 97% (161) (Table 3). Overall, 103 (62%) patients experienced Grade ≥3 TRAEs. TRAEs frequently led to dose modifications, with 75% resulting in dose interruption or reduction. Specifically, 36% of patients had dose interruptions, and 66% had dose reductions due to TRAEs. Permanent discontinuation due to TRAEs occurred in 8% of patients. Among the most common TRAEs (incidence ≥10%), peripheral oedema was reported in 63% of patients, followed by aspartate aminotransferase increased (43%) and alanine aminotransferase increased (42%). Frequently reported Grade ≥3 TRAEs were hepatic function abnormal (17%), alanine aminotransferase increased (16%), and aspartate aminotransferase increased (12%). Three (2%) patients experienced TRAEs leading to death. These included cardiac failure and unknown reasons as previously published,16 as well as a new case of pneumonia. The death due to pneumonia was confounded by the primary tumour and multiple underlying comorbidities, including hypoalbuminemia, pleural effusion, and others. Detailed overviews of TEAEs and TRAEs with an incidence ≥10% are provided for the total population and individual cohorts in Table 3 and Supplementary Tables S8–S12. Dose adjustments and treatment interruptions are summarised in Supplementary Table S13. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This final analysis of the largest study of METex14-mutated NSCLC in Asian patients confirms the long-term survival benefits of savolitinib in locally advanced or metastatic disease. With the longer follow-up in this final analysis, the PFS was mature, and the median PFS was both 13·7 months in the previously treated cohort and the treatment-naïve cohort; median OS reached 25·3 months and 28·3 months, respectively, highlighting long-term benefits. Of note, our findings show comparable PFS in the previously treated cohort and the treatment-naïve cohort, while capmatinib showed contrasting outcomes between cohorts.9 This may have been influenced by the higher proportion of younger patients in our previously treated group (39% versus 22% < 65 years).16,17

Subgroup results of patients with brain metastases supported the long-term benefits of savolitinib, with most patients achieving shrunken or stable intracranial lesions and few patients (three in the previously treated cohort) experiencing intracranial progression. Molecular characterization revealed that the specific molecular architecture of METex14 alterations did not significantly influence clinical outcomes, supporting the therapeutic consistency reported across diverse MET alteration subtypes in earlier investigations.15

Previous savolitinib studies have reported a 50% frequency of TP53 mutations in ctDNA samples from patients with pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma (PSC), compared with 22·7% in other subtypes of NSCLC.19 Another comprehensive analysis of 65 patients harbouring METex14 mutations (24 PSC and 41 NSCLC cases) demonstrated an overall TP53 co-mutation prevalence of 49% in tissue specimens, with rates of 62·5% and 41·5% in PSC and NSCLC,15 respectively—marginally higher than ctDNA-based reports. In our study, TP53 co-mutations were detected in 30% of baseline ctDNA samples. Considering the limited number of PSC cases (N = 5) in our cohort, the aggregate TP53 mutation frequency aligns with previously published data. Regarding the influence of TP53 co-mutations in blood samples on treatment efficacy, the present study did not detect statistically significant differences in ORR, PFS, or OS between patients harbouring mutated versus wild-type TP53. This observation remained consistent across the whole population and in subgroup analyses of previously treated and treatment-naïve populations.

When comparing the present efficacy results with previous studies,9,10,12 the observed response and survival are broadly comparable to those reported for tepotinib in the VISION trial (ORR 50% and 59%, PFS 11·5 and 15·9 months, OS 20·4 and 29·7 months in the previously treated and treatment-naïve cohorts, respectively) and capmatinib in the GEOMETRY mono-1 trial (ORR 44% and 68%, PFS 5·5 and 12·5 months, OS 16·8 and 21·4 months for treatment-naïve and previously treated cohorts, respectively). However, direct comparisons with other agents such as capmatinib and tepotinib should be made cautiously. Nevertheless, the overall efficacy profile of savolitinib remains consistent with global findings for MET inhibitors, reinforcing its therapeutic potential.

Regarding safety, savolitinib was well-tolerated and its safety profile was manageable within the study population after the long-term follow-up. Its safety profile was consistent with the primary analysis16,17 and known risks from previous studies and other drugs in the same class,9,10 with no new safety signals identified. Aspartate aminotransferase increased and alanine aminotransferase increased were the most frequently reported events, most events were Grade 1 or 2, and no deaths were related to these events. The Grade ≥3 TRAEs were primarily hepatic, manageable via dose modifications, and resulted in low discontinuation rates (≤2% due to hepatic events).

MET alterations include MET mutations, MET amplification, and MET overexpression. In addition to METex14 mutations, MET amplification/overexpression is a key resistance pathway after progression on EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Savolitinib is now being evaluated to overcome MET-mediated resistance in EGFR-mutated NSCLC, with trials such as SACHI20 and SAVANNAH21 providing promising evidence for combination therapy.

This study had some limitations. Because of the low incidence of METex14 mutations (3%–4%)1 and a lack of approved targeted comparators at the time of design, this study adopted a single-arm design for confirmatory purposes, an approach consistent with regulatory pathways for other MET inhibitors.9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 This may have potentially introduced bias. To mitigate this, an IRC was established, and the IRC-assessed ORR was the primary endpoint. Additionally, this study specifically targeted the Chinese population, potentially limiting its generalisability. The efficacy results for the subgroup of patients with brain metastases were promising; however, these results should be interpreted with caution, as these findings are exploratory and the study was not powered to assess efficacy in this subgroup. Moreover, because ctDNA sample collection at end of treatment was not mandatory, the limited number of samples collected at this point precluded comprehensive exploration of resistance mechanisms. Finally, wide CIs should be expected owing to the small sample sizes.

In conclusion, patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with METex14 mutations may obtain favourable clinical benefit from treatment with savolitinib. With proven efficacy and manageable risks, savolitinib could be used as a standard of care for this population.
